resources.string: Each engine keeps its own parameters — pick one to view or change them.
Editing %1$s [%2$s]. In Compare, each tier applies only its own (and only what it supports, see TierCapabilities).
Use this configuration on all engines
To compare with identical parameters. Only what each engine supports is copied; the rest is left untouched.
Randomness of the answer. Close to 0: always picks the most likely word (predictable, repetitive). Close to 2: tries less likely options (more creative, but may ramble).
At each word, the model can only choose among the K most likely options. Low K (e.g. 5) = more conservative answers; high K = more variety.

Similar to Top-K, but instead of a fixed number of options it cuts off when the cumulative probability reaches P (e.g. 0.95 = the options that add up to 95% probability). Many backends combine Top-K and Top-P.
Cap on the length of the answer, in tokens (~4 characters each, approximate). The model may finish earlier on its own; this is a ceiling, not a target.
System prompt (not supported on this tier)

Instruction given to the model before each prompt, to set its role or answer style (e.g. \"Always answer in 2 sentences\"). It is added to a fixed context that already tells the model what nanodemo is, on all 5 tiers.

Asks the model to return JSON instead of free text. Cloud and Firebase AI guarantee it (the API\'s responseMimeType); Nano/MediaPipe/LiteRT-LM emulate it through the prompt (no syntactic guarantee, it depends on the model complying). Chat flags whether the answer ended up being valid JSON, on all 5 tiers.

Lets the model ask for the current time in a time zone instead of making it up — it has no clock of its own. Cloud and Firebase AI do it natively (the API has real tool-calling); Nano/MediaPipe/LiteRT-LM emulate it through the prompt (less reliable: it depends on the model following the requested format). Chat shows when it was used.

Searches the internet before answering, for current questions the model cannot know. Cloud/Firebase AI use native grounding (the API\'s own Google Search; the model decides when). Nano/MediaPipe/LiteRT-LM have no network of their own: with this on, the app ALWAYS searches (Brave Search API), reads an excerpt of the first pages and hands it to the model, which answers with formatting, citing [1], [2] and with a clickable list of sources below. BRAVE_SEARCH_API_KEY must be configured, otherwise it stays disabled. If you also turned on Tools, this one wins (they were not tested together).
Local counter of what you spend on each free plan. It only covers this app and this device: it does not replace the spending caps in the Google/Brave consoles.
No limit: Nano, MediaPipe and LiteRT-LM (on-device), pasting a link and the semantic search of the history run on the phone and use no quota.

Web search on Cloud/Firebase AI (grounding with Google Search): not included in the Gemini free plan — a paid plan is required (5,000 searches/month free, then $14 per 1,000). Without a paid plan, turning that toggle on for those tiers may fail.
Limit reached (warning only: blocking is turned off).
Block when the limit is reached
Free plan: limits per PROJECT (not per key), no card. Every HTTP call counts (a turn with tools or search makes 2). No grounding on the free plan.

Gemini Developer API through Firebase (Spark plan, no card). If the Tier C key belongs to the SAME project, they share quota: split the limit between the two. Linking billing (Blaze) makes everything paid.
Brave Search · search for the local tiers
$5 monthly credit ≈ 1000 searches; beyond that Brave charges $5 per 1000.
